title: Trump Administration Narrows H-1B Hiring With Layoff Scrutiny and New Fees
excerpt: A September 18 executive order makes an employer's layoffs in the past year a factor in H-1B reviews, alongside an extended $100,000 payment for hires from abroad and a proposal to end the 60-day job-loss grace period.
body:
• A September 18 executive order directs Homeland Security, Labor and State to take an employer's layoffs in the previous year into account when reviewing H-1B labor condition applications, petitions, visas and entry.
  • The order does not ban H-1B hiring after layoffs, and attorneys say an outright denial based only on job cuts would likely be challenged in court.
  • The $100,000 payment for H-1B hires from outside the United States has been extended through September 21, 2027, though courts have blocked agency guidance implementing it, and DHS has proposed ending the 60-day grace period after a job loss.
  • For readers: if you hold H-1B status and lose your job today, the up-to-60-day grace period is still in place — comments on ending it close November 10, 2026 — but an employer that laid off workers in the past year should expect closer scrutiny of its next filing.

The Trump administration has added layoffs to the facts federal agencies must weigh when an employer seeks to hire on an H-1B visa, the latest step in a sequence of orders, proclamations and proposed rules that attorneys say is narrowing the path for hiring skilled workers from abroad. Law.com, in an October 2 analysis, described the measures as showing that push continuing, with little recourse for employers.

Under the September 18 executive order, State, Labor and Homeland Security must coordinate with Commerce, Education and the Small Business Administration, and must take into account whether a sponsor engaged in layoffs within the previous year, or plans future layoffs, affecting similarly situated United States workers. The White House said technology employers requested H-1B visas for hundreds of thousands of workers while laying off 800,000 to 1.3 million American employees from 2022 through 2026.

Layoffs Become a Compliance Signal, Not a Ban

Most employers are not barred from adding foreign workers after cutting positions, Bloomberg Law reported. Only a sliver face similar displacement restrictions for H-1B hiring, among them companies with 15 percent or more of their workforce in H-1B status. Stricter obligations apply in the PERM green-card process after layoffs in the previous six months.

https://x.com/DallasExpress/status/2113658535288414464

"Employers that haven't traditionally had to consider displacement in the H-1B process should be thinking really hard about it and doing a risk analysis."

— Edward Raleigh, partner at Fragomen, Del Rey, Bernsen & Loewy LLP, told Bloomberg Law

The order directed the Department of Labor, within 30 days, to review previously submitted labor condition applications. L.J. D'Arrigo of Harris Beach Murtha told Bloomberg Law reviews could look for heavy use of entry-level wages, work sites that do not match Homeland Security petitions, and large filing volumes by firms placing workers at third-party sites.

A Stack of Parallel Restrictions

The layoff order arrived the same day as a proclamation extending the $100,000 payment for hires from outside the United States through September 21, 2027. The White House said the payment had been made for over 700 petitions since September 2025, and registrations by the largest IT staffing firms had fallen from 24,946 to 2,055. A federal judge in California has since blocked agencies from implementing guidance under the fee proclamation until notice-and-comment rulemaking takes place, according to Bloomberg Law.

Two other proposals add to the pressure. Homeland Security has proposed a new six-figure fee for cap-subject H-1B petitions, Bloomberg Law reported, and, according to Reuters, a Federal Register proposal to eliminate the 60-day grace period, in place since 2017, that lets H-1B workers remain after a job loss while they find a new sponsor. The Labor Department's Project Firewall initiative has also put alleged fraud under closer examination.

What It Means for Indian Professionals

Indian professionals account for a significant share of H-1B holders, concentrated in technology, People Matters reported. The layoff order does not change eligibility by itself, but Anne Rowley of Grossman Young & Hammond told Bloomberg Law layoff histories could lead Homeland Security to issue more requests for evidence on future petitions.

Some attorneys doubt the order will change outcomes for large technology employers. George Fishman of the Center for Immigration Studies told Bloomberg Law companies denied on layoff grounds alone would sue and most likely win, and attorney Jonathan Wasden said the order was unlikely to lead to much beyond signaling. The order must be implemented consistent with existing law and, by its own terms, creates no enforceable rights.

What's Next

Agencies must now translate the directives into guidance, and the Labor Department's review of earlier applications is the first test of how aggressively they will use it. The grace-period proposal remains open for comment until November 10, 2026, and the $100,000 payment remains contested in court. Employers filing after recent layoffs should expect longer, more document-heavy reviews rather than a single new prohibition.
